Pass 17's gain is mostly better reasoning, not just stopping loops. Of the 49 wrong→right answers under S3, 38 were finished-but-wrong answers in the original and only 11 were cut-offs. Most former cut-offs (43 of 63) became finished but still wrong.

The R1a edit is saved and backed up. It projects only the spike direction out of head 3's output columns, which removes 19% of that block's energy (block norm 15.92 → 14.36) and leaves heads 0–2 bit-identical.

I now run the paired generation on DEV[1024:1250], the slice where S3 (head 3 ×0.2) gave +18.6.
- If R1a gives a comparable gain, the single spike direction is the brake.
- If it gives little or nothing, the damage comes from head 3's main write, and I will tune whole-head damping instead.

R1a, removing only head 3's spike direction, does nothing: −0.9 ± 1.9 points (8 wrong→right, 10 right→wrong), with cut-offs slightly up (28% → 32%). So the volume-knob idea is refuted: the rank-1 spike, which writes into dimensions the norm discards, is not the brake. The +18.6 from S3 (head 3 ×0.2) must come from reducing head 3's main write, which after the norm is 3–6× larger than its siblings'.

The next decision-relevant question is the dose: is head 3 harmful all the way down (×0 better than ×0.2), or does it also carry something useful (×0 worse)? I therefore set up S3 ×0, a full ablation of head 3's output columns, for the same slice DEV[1024:1250], directly comparable to ×0.2 (+18.6) and R1a (−0.9).
- If ×0 ≥ ×0.2, head 3 is net harmful and ablation is the clean undo.
- If ×0 is clearly worse, the head has a useful part, and I would look for the harmful subspace or settle on an intermediate strength.

While setting this up, I also print weight forensics comparing head 3's output and query blocks with its siblings (norms and spectrum quantiles). A planted uniform scale-up would show as a uniformly raised bulk.

The weight forensics show head 3's output block is larger across its whole spectrum, not only at the spike. Its mid and bulk singular values are about 1.3–2× its siblings': s[10] = 1.65 against 0.82–1.13, s[50] = 1.10 against 0.59–0.84, s[128] = 0.72 against 0.38–0.57. Its query block has larger top directions (6.21 and 4.60, against at most 5.06 and 3.51) but an ordinary bulk.

This fits the R1a result: the head's whole write is oversized, not one direction. Whole-head damping is therefore the natural repair, and the remaining question is the dose.

The S3 ×0 edit (head 3 output columns zeroed, heads 0–2 untouched) is saved, backed up and logged. I now run it paired on DEV[1024:1250], the same slice as ×0.2 (+18.6) and R1a (−0.9).
- If ×0 is at least as good as ×0.2, head 3 is net harmful and full ablation is the undo.
- If it is clearly worse, the head carries something useful and the best strength lies between 0 and 1.

Fully ablating head 3 helps, but less than damping it. Head 3 ×0 gives +11.1 ± 3.0 (37 wrong→right, 12 right→wrong): accuracy 29.6%, cut-offs 2.2%, mean answer length 172 tokens. On the same slice and the same original answers, ×0.2 gave +18.6 (accuracy 37.2%, 209 tokens).

So head 3 is not pure harm: it carries a useful function, and its oversized write is what holds the model back. The dose curve on DEV[1024:1250] so far:

| Edit | Paired change |
|---|---|
| ×1 (original) | 0 |
| ×0.2 | +18.6 |
| ×0 | +11.1 |
| spike-only removal | −0.9 |

This peaked shape fits the weight forensics: head 3's whole spectrum is 1.3–1.7× its siblings', and its post-norm write is 3–6× theirs. A strength of roughly 0.2–0.35 would bring it to sibling scale.

To locate the peak on the other side, I now test ×0.5 on the same slice.
- If ×0.5 is about as good as ×0.2 (+15 to +19), the optimum is broad and lies around 0.3.
- If it drops clearly (below about +10), the optimum is near 0.2.
